threads.title: Teeny Tiny Homes
threads.body:
Everything to Know About Building or Buying a Tiny Home
Interest continues to grow for minimalist, often mobile, houses with no room to spare.
By Dina Cheney
Tiny homes are small, but the consumer interest in them is large and growing. The market is expected to increase from $13.17 billion in 2025 to $14 billion this year, according to Research and Markets.
Usually measuring from 100 to 400 square feet, these homes offer novelty, charm, flexibility and low cost. However, because tiny homes don’t fit neatly into established categories — like recreational vehicles (R.V.s), mobile homes, accessory dwelling units (A.D.U.s) or traditional houses — they often face zoning and placement barriers.
Costing as little as $30,000, tiny homes are among the most affordable types of housing. Built like traditional homes, with framing and insulation, they’re made for year-round living, said Jenna Kausal, host of the YouTube channel, “Tiny House Giant Journey,” which has nearly 2 million subscribers.

threads.author: aRebelsReckoning
threads.body:
Living a different kind of life these days.
I work long shifts as a live-in caregiver, staying 10 days at a time in someone else’s home. On my days off, I climb into my little Minnie Winnie and wander eastern Oklahoma. Some nights I park in my mamma’s yard, some nights at a casino, Walmart, or wherever feels quiet enough to rest. Then I head back and do it all again.
It’s not always easy, but it’s honest.
Lately tension has been building around where my RV is parked while I’m working. Harsh words were thrown before peaceful conversation was ever attempted, and accusations are now being used to justify resentment that apparently has been sitting for months. Truth mixed with anger can still become cruelty.
So I’ll simply move on.
No screaming match. No revenge. No victim story. Just another reminder that sometimes the only peace available is the peace created by leaving quietly.
That little RV may not look like much to most people, but it’s my freedom, my reset button, and sometimes the only place that feels fully mine.

threads.title: The Little Rituals That Prepare You for Sleep
threads.body:
(I'm sure you've heard that one thing to combat insomnia is to have a little pre-bed ritual.)
The Little Rituals That Prepare You for Sleep
Origami, cleaning countertops, talking to plants — here are some ways readers wind down for the evening.
By Amanda Schupak
Consistent evening routines, including keeping regular bedtimes and engaging in calming activities like meditation and breathing exercises, have been shown to improve sleep quality. Last month, we asked readers to tell us about their nightly habits. More than 1,100 people responded.
I like to polish my granite kitchen countertops with a green-apple-smelling cleaner. There’s something therapeutic about seeing the liquid hitting the counter and the smell of fresh green apples hitting your nostrils. It just completes my day.
Art Rosales, 55, Ventura, Calif.
After getting ready for bed, I walk around my house and talk to my plants. I see if they need water, have any new growth, need a little fertilizer. I’ll often share my worries or hopes for the next day with them. It helps me find some peace before getting into bed.
Billy Farrell, 34, Anchorage
Recently I received two books about origami. Attempting a new origami figure each night in bed before shutting off the light is rewarding and fun, and helps me wind down.
Christina, 62, Toronto
My husband and I work on a 1,500-piece puzzle (we have a special puzzle board that swivels and has drawers for sorting) and watch “Antiques Roadshow.”
Sarah Lerner, 32, Durham, N.C.
For about 20 minutes in the evening, my family and I walk “the circle”: a path that runs through the living room, dining and kitchen area, then through the foyer back into the living room. It’s a walking meditation of sorts and helps burn through any lingering thoughts that might obstruct a good night’s sleep.
Boz Killebrew, 53, Oregon, Wis.
Sometimes I read a cookbook in bed to get ideas for what to make during the week.
Randall Reade, 64, Washington, D.C.
I do a crossword, then I turn off the lights and turn on “Law and Order” with a sleep timer. Seasons one through 11 — the newer seasons don’t seem to work!
Gail Noren, 57, Alexandria, Va.
My partner and I lie down facing each other, hold hands and look into each other’s eyes. We then share something about our day, how we’re feeling or just something we love about each other. It is supremely affirming and relaxing and always gives me that warm feeling I remember from the first time I told her that I loved her.
Andrew Dunakin, 56, Wyndmoor, Pa.
For the whole list:

threads.title: At Kennedy Center, the mice matter
threads.author: creigalt2
threads.body:
At Kennedy Center, the mice matter.
The Lonely Crew at the Kennedy Center Will Miss Its…Mice
Skittles, a mouse that has made a home at the Kennedy Center, was nicknamed by stagehands
Employees say the performing arts center’s quirky-looking mice have an exotic back story
By Elizabeth Williamson
President Trump’s takeover of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts has left the building nearly empty. So the few lonely staff members who remain ahead of a potential two-year closure this month for renovations are prone to sharing tales of what for 50 years has made the place special.
Like the mice.
Kennedy Center mice do not resemble the typical gray house mice found in fields and woods in warmer weather and in kitchens and attics when it’s cold. They are roughly half that size, with large ears and fur of a golden tan color that, if they were horses, would be called palomino. Their bellies are pearl white.
For years stagehands have spotted a tan mouse — or maybe alternating mice — sitting motionless beneath a wheelchair ramp facing one of the center’s two Millennium Stages, seemingly watching the evening shows...
The Kennedy Center was built as a living memorial to the slain President John F. Kennedy, a patron of the arts who championed its construction. Amid a surge of grief and tribute after his assassination in 1963, more than 60 nations donated furnishings and artwork to the center rising on the Potomac.
The largest of these gifts came from Italy: 3,700 tons of dazzling white Carrara marble for the facade and interior walls, specially mined in Tuscany’s Apuan Alps, in the same area as the marble for Michelangelo’s David. The region is home to the Alpine field mouse and its genetic kin. threads.title: Rice Noodles with Chicken and Broccoli!
threads.author: absolutefutility
threads.body:
I was looking forward to finding a good use for the 12 boxes of rice noodles I scooped up from Amazon. I'm gently trying to reduce the amount of gluten in my diet.
I'd only made the rice noodles once before and they were actually a different version than these. Those were tiny little strands and they only needed to be soaked in hot water for about 10 minutes to be ready to use. I tried doing that with these and they...weren't. I eventually had to read the box and it said they needed to soak in boiling water for about 6 minutes and then, very quickly, you have to drain them and run cold water over them to stop them from falling apart.
This last step is essential and is easily overlooked.
Before all of that, though, I knew I wanted to have a simple sort of stir-fry dinner. I couldn't choose between chicken and shrimp but eventually just went with the chicken because it was thawed and the shrimp was still frozen.
I sauteed some onions and some diced broccoli together in peanut oil and some Nature's Seasons until it was tender. Then I set it aside and did the same with the diced chicken. Once the chicken was done, I added it to the vegetables and started on the sauce.
The sauce is one I invented myself based on one I'd seen on Youtube. The sauce is the "2x2 sauce". We can call it "Noah" sauce. If you know, you know! The way it works is that you just take TWO tablespoons of each ingredient.
This is a guideline and not a rule since I didn't actually have two tablespoons of a few ingredients.
I started with two tablespoons of:
Brown sugar
Minced Garlic
Soy Sauce
Tempura Sauce
Teriyaki Sauce
Fish Sauce (or Oyster Sauce)
Hoisin Sauce
Sesame Oil
And then I switched to just ONE tablespoon of each of the following:
Worcestershire Sauce
White Wine Vinegar
Balsamic Vinegar
Peanut Oil
Anchovy Essence
Ketchup
I kept the number even so it was within the bounds of the guidelines of the sauce. You probably could have done two tablespoons of each, but I didn't have two tablespoons left of the Vinegar or Anchovy Essence.
I put them in the pot that I'd used to cook everything and brought it to the boil. Then this is the tricky part. It bubbled away happily for a quarter of an hour...but it didn't really thicken as much as I thought it should. I probably would have added cornstarch if I realized how thin it was at the time, but I didn't. So I'd recommend that now.
The sauce boiled for a bit then I added the noodles and stirred them through until they were well coated in the sauce. Then I added in the mix of chicken and veggies and stirred it through until everything was coated and heated.
It was very nice, tasty, simple. I'll be adding this to my regular rotation now, although I'll switch to shrimp in the next effort.

threads.title: Rice Noodles Verdict...
threads.author: Pigshot
threads.body:
I asked AI "Is this post really that bad?" and it found 20 faults, but here is the final verdict:
The post is not "that bad." It's a solid, enthusiastic recipe post with helpful tips and a clever sauce concept. However, it could be improved by tightening the structure, adding more specific cooking instructions, reducing the sauce complexity, and explaining why the dish was successful. A reader who follows this post exactly might end up with a thin sauce, overcooked chicken, or mushy noodles—but if they read carefully and use common sense, they'll likely make a tasty meal.
Check out #14: Too "cutesy" LOL
Weaknesses:
1. The opening is abrupt. "I was looking forward to finding a good use for the 12 boxes of rice noodles I scooped up from Amazon" assumes the reader knows about the writer's previous posts. For a new reader, this is confusing.
2. The phrase "I'm gently trying to reduce the amount of gluten in my diet" is vague. "Gently" suggests the writer isn't fully committed. Is this a medical need or a preference? The ambiguity undermines the urgency of the post.
3. The noodle preparation section is confusing. The writer says they "tried doing that with these and they...weren't." The ellipsis is meant to be humorous, but it's unclear what happened. Did they fall apart? Were they undercooked? The reader is left guessing.
4. The transition from noodles to the stir-fry is jarring. The writer says "Before all of that, though, I knew I wanted to have a simple sort of stir-fry dinner." This should have come earlier.
5. The writer says they "couldn't choose between chicken and shrimp" but chose chicken because it was thawed. This is a minor detail that doesn't add much.
6. The vegetable preparation is too brief. "I sauteed some onions and some diced broccoli together in peanut oil" tells the reader nothing about time, temperature, or desired texture. Were the onions caramelized? Was the broccoli tender-crisp? The reader has no idea.
7. The same issue applies to the chicken. "Once the chicken was done" is vague. Was it browned? Cooked through? How did the writer know it was done?
8. The sauce section is the heart of the post, but it's poorly organized. The writer lists ingredients, then admits they didn't follow their own rule, then recommends cornstarch as a thickener. This reads as stream-of-consciousness rather than a recipe.
9. The list formatting is inconsistent. The first list uses colons and the second uses dashes. This is a minor issue, but it makes the post feel rushed.
10. The "2x2 sauce" name is clever, but the writer undermines it by immediately saying "This is a guideline and not a rule since I didn't actually have two tablespoons of a few ingredients." This makes the reader wonder: is the sauce consistent, or is it always improvised?
11. The writer mentions "Noah sauce" and says "If you know, you know!" This is an inside joke that will alienate readers who don't get the reference.
12. The sauce recipe is too long and complicated. Fourteen ingredients for a simple stir-fry is excessive. A reader looking for a quick weeknight dinner might be overwhelmed.
13. The writer admits the sauce didn't thicken as expected and recommends cornstarch, but this recommendation is buried. It should have been included in the instructions, not as an afterthought.
14. The phrase "It bubbled away happily for a quarter of an hour" is unnecessarily cutesy. "Quarter of an hour" is also an odd way to say "15 minutes."
15. The assembly section is rushed. "I added the noodles and stirred them through until they were well coated" is a single sentence. The reader would benefit from more detail—did the noodles absorb the sauce? Did the chicken and vegetables stay separate?
16. The final verdict ("It was very nice, tasty, simple") is generic. The writer doesn't explain what made it nice. Was it the sweetness of the brown sugar? The umami of the fish sauce? The reader is told the dish was good but not why.
17. The post is too long for its content. The writer spends 500+ words on a simple stir-fry with a complicated sauce. A tighter version would cut the digressions and focus on the essentials.
18. The title is slightly misleading. "Rice Noodles with Chicken and Broccoli!" suggests the dish is simple, but the sauce recipe is anything but. The title sets an expectation that the post doesn't quite meet.
19. The post lacks photos. A recipe post like this would greatly benefit from a picture of the finished dish.
20. The writer never mentions portion sizes. How many servings did this make? The reader has no way to scale the recipe.

First useful suggestion, in gray:
The usb ports might be simply going to sleep... and your device is not waking them up. Check that first.
Then try power cycling the laptop for real to fix usb ports when they are off (driver problem) by holding the power button until the laptop shuts down (don't do this too often). Next, remove the battery and remove the power adapter plug from the laptop.
Next, hold the power button for 5 seconds.
Then insert the battery and reconnect the power (if needed), and start the laptop. The usb ports should be working again.
I tried this. Worked perfectly! But next morning the USB ports were dead again. And I'm wondering about the warning not to do this too often.
Second useful suggestion, from m00vieluvr
A few things to check:
1. Device Manager
* Look under:
* Universal Serial Bus Controllers
* See if anything shows:
* yellow warning icons
* “Unknown USB Device”
* Try uninstalling the USB Root Hub/controller and rebooting.
2. Disable USB Power Saving
In Windows:
* Control Panel → Power Options
* Change Plan Settings
* Advanced Power Settings
* USB Settings
* Disable:
* USB Selective Suspend
Also in Device Manager:
* USB Root Hub → Properties → Power Management
* Uncheck:
* “Allow the computer to turn off this device to save power”
3. Check BIOS/UEFI
Some newer laptops have aggressive USB security/power settings:
* USB Sleep Charging
* Modern Standby
* USB Security
* Thunderbolt security modes
4. Chipset Drivers
A lot of “USB randomly dies” issues are actually Intel/AMD chipset driver problems. If the machine only occasionally goes online, it may suddenly start working after Windows Update refreshes those drivers.
I did find the USB Root Hub and unclicked the box about turning off to save power. At one point I saw an orange triangle, but it didn't say if there was a particular problem.

threads.title: you shouldn't need to update
threads.author: never-online---
threads.body:
The suggestions by that other poster are good. 100% the suggestion about the power turning off the USB ports is spot on as one cause of issues. Other things too - about device drivers - make 100% sense as a cause.
But with all of that, once you change something, the problem shouldn't return ... unless you or someone else is actively doing what is called a Restore, which resets the operating system to the state it was in a few months ago. But someone has to consciously do that. And the person doing that would see that happen. You can't do it accidentally and not know it. And you would find any changes (including documents you'd written) would be gone and you'd be back to the way it was a few months ago.
But first question is what do you mean by update? Because right now (and starting in November 2025), there aren't any normal system updates from Microsoft if your computer is Windows 10 and anything earlier like Windows 8 or 7 wouldn't even have anything new to update.
But I'm going to assume because you can't answer immediately that you don't know what is being updated, but maybe you can describe what you press to get this update.
But putting that aside for a moment, USB is dead at one point and then later it is working, so it can't be a physical problem. A toaster or microwave that is fried and dead, is fried today and fried tomorrow and doesn't work no matter what. A loose wire for a toaster will produce inconsistent results and requires a physical fix and that's not what updating does, so this is not a physical problem.
Just out of curiosity, though, when you say it's dead and it's dead in your presence, what happens if you plug in a USB mouse or keyboard, if you have one. You said it doesn't read anything, but I'm guessing you really mean just a USB drive and not really anything as in other things plugged in like a mouse. USB mouse would have a light somewhere on it if you plug it in and move around. USB data doesn't work, does anything else? If it does work, you jiggle the usb mouse and the mouse arrow moves around the screen.
Next when you say plugged in nothing works, is that an assumption based on one and only one USB drive? Because what you describe could possibly be explained by a USB being determined as a problem by micosoft's antivirus.
Something that does get updated every so often or is recommended to be ... as in once every few months, is antivirus. That would still be updated on your laptop. So is your antivirus the thing that is updated every few months when you go online and once antivirus is updated, that fixes the USB drive?
Even that doesn't explain everything as you describe it. Could be multiple issues that you combine together or something else. A USB drive could be blocked, but an antivirus update should not unblock it. You'd also get some kind of warning about that the USB drive was unsafe.
m00vieluvr wrote a suggestion about checking the BIOS. You have no idea what that is. BIOS is an acronym that stands for Basic Input Output ....?system? I forget what the S stands for. Most of the time it looks like a 1980s computer on the screen - black screen and white text and options half of which have acronyms you won't what they mean even when you find out what the acronyms spells out.
So I'm guessing when you wrote in response to m00vieluvr 'Thanks', you didn't really do everything he suggested. That's not a condemnation of you. I'm just trying to determine what was done.
m00vieluvr wrote about taking out the battery and reinstalling and you did that. That would not fix anything directly with antivirus, but what taking out the battery does is for a laptop is typically to reset the clock to the original factory date and get rid of any non-standard BIOS settings - which could be something to do with USB ports and power efficiency.
So you had to reset the date after you took out the battery? The clock/date is typically in the bottom right of the screen.

threads.title: Plague Tale...
threads.author: absolutefutility
threads.body:
I've had this game for a long time on my PS4 but never played it. It wasn't really in the list of games that I thought I would enjoy playing so it just languished in the back catalogue.
I knew, objectively, that it shared the DNA of a game I had on the PS3 called Amy and if you look up that game, you'll see that the characters look very much like the main characters, Amicia and Hugo, from A Plague Tale. And that was really the problem because Amy was buggy as hell and it was so bad that even the walkthrough and guide videos showed that you had to get eaten by zombies and reload your game in a lot of places just to progress through the game!
A Plague Tale shares some of these mechanics and some of those same bugs.
The story is about a girl called Amicia who has a younger brother named Hugo. Hugo has been ill for his entire life, tended to by their mother. Amicia is close with her father and rarely sees her mother.
Then, one day, there's an attack in the woods and the Inquisition shows up and wants Hugo for some nefarious reason.
From that point onward, Amicia is "guiding" Hugo to some fabled "safe place" for them to escape the Inquisition and get on with their lives.
But, no, of course, there's more...
While the Inquisition is going through France ruining people's lives...so is the plague...and these rats that are spreading it are actually controlled by magic. Hugo is also infected with whatever it is that is controlling the rats and that means they end up following him around as they try to escape.
But, again, remember when I said this was buggy? The rats are supposed to be scared of light and fire but the game is so buggy that sometimes they forget...and they also forget that they are trapped behind objects. So, you'll be going along, using fire and light to protect yourself and then, the next thing you know, you're instantly killed by a swarm of rats that, I dunno, have suddenly gone blind...
And this happens a lot.
By the end of the first game, Hugo has more control over the rats and you can use that to mercilessly murder the people who keep wanting to mercilessly murder you.
But then you get to the second game.
This game is way more buggy than the first (but not as buggy as Amy). With this game, Hugo and Amicia have rescued their mother from the Inquisition and made it somewhere safe. Hugo is still suffering and will probably die, but he is now having dreams that there's an island he can go to that will cure him.
The rats attack and off you go again, doing the same stupid things with the same buggy game running away from the same buggy rats.
BUT! Now there's another problem; the game will spontaneously send you error messages telling you that your PS5 is overheated.
And, of course, you're concerned because your PS5 shouldn't be overheating!
And it isn't...
No one seems to know why the game is throwing up those errors. But they're just errors because they will come up repeatedly - you can REPEAT the error - over and over, in exact locations throughout the game. The only thing I can intuit about this problem is that, while the game is "PS5 Pro Enhanced", I think it must not be "properly" enhanced so it goes to load a texture or do something that the standard PS5 can't do and the system reads that error as the same thing that would happen if the console had overheated and it kicks up the error message.
But it hasn't overheated and if you hit the circle button and back out of the error message, it goes away. But if you RELOAD the level, you'll get the error again. Over and over.
Like I said...BUG-GY!
Other than the fact that the game has serious issues, it is very pretty. The first game was way more difficult because it didn't have any accessibility settings. The second game does have them, and you can play just for the story - which is what I like to do, since gaming should be fun and not tedious - but they screwed up the armory controls for no reason.
In the first game you didn't have any weapons except a sling and you had to keep collecting rocks. In this game you don't have to collect rocks anymore and you get a crossbow...but you can only ever have two bolts!
Like most games, you've forgotten all your crafting from the first game and zero reason is ever given for why you can't craft the things you were able to craft in the last game. They think they made up for that by giving you the crossbow, but, seriously, TWO bolts!? Half the time you have to use the bolts to light your way through the rats so what is the point?
The game could have been so much better but, damn, I don't know what they were thinking when they went with the "you can't run, you can't hide, and you can't fight" method...it pretty much sucks!
Still, Amy was impossible to finish. When the guides are telling you: "get eaten by zombies, die, and reload your game and then you can progress", you know that someone was really phoning it in for a paycheck.
A Plague Tale one and two were both free for me, but I certainly wouldn't have paid to play them.
